newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia 1997 GDP seen at 7.8-8.2 pct, Negara says.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia 1997 GDP seen at 7.8-8.2 pct, Negara says.

text.p: Malaysia's gross domestic product (GDP) is expected to grow between 7.8 and 8.2 percent in 1997 against 8.2 percent last year, Bank Negara said on Friday in its 1996 annual report.
Malaysia brought down growth from a peak of 9.5 percent in 1995, responding to fears of overheating and aided by a slowdown in the global electrical and electronics market, the central bank said.
"The GDP will grow by around eight percent," a spokesperson for Bank Negara said at the presentation of the annual report.

"If the external sector recovery is less, then it (growth) could be lower, and if it is more then it could be slightly higher, but it will be within the narrow range. But all computations are for eight percent," she said.
The downside uncertainty for the economy is how well the electrical and electronics industry recovers from last year's slump, the central bank report said.
The sector accounts for two-thirds of Malaysia's manufacturing exports and attracts the bulk of foreign investment.
"All major sectors of the economy are expected to expand further in 1997, although the pace of growth in most sectors would be slower than in 1996," the report said.
Growth in the manufacturing sector is expected to be around 11 percent in 1997 against 12 percent last year.

"In particular, the performance of the electronics and electrical industry is expected to improve. The world chip market is forecast to grow by 7.4 percent after a sharp decline in sales by 10.5 percent in 1996," the report said.

The Multimedia Super Corridor, a zone south of Kuala Lumpur which Malaysia is building for information technology companies, and the launch later this year of a new over-the-counter market to help finance fledgling, high-tech firms, would also boost growth, the report said.
But the withdrawal of preferential tariffs under the U.S. Generalised System of Preferences "may have some negative impact on exports of consumer electrical goods", it said.

"Although the United States is the largest market for electronics and electrical products, the increasing diversification into Japan and the Asia-Pacific region is expected to moderate any significant reduction in demand."
Growth in the construction sector is expected to remain at 13 percent, with the biggest impetus coming from ongoing and planned infrastructure projects, the report said.
These include the giant Bakun dam in the Borneo state of Sarawak, the West Coast highway, and a new monorail transport system in Kuala Lumpur.
The services sector is projected to grow by 9.0 percent in 1997.

"The transport, storage and communications sub-sector is expected to continue to record strong growth, benefiting from the capacity expansion programmes of the national airline and shipping lines, as well as investments by telecommunications companies," the report said.
Growth in the agriculture and mining sectors is expected to moderate to 2.0 percent and 2.1 percent respectively.
Crude palm oil output will grow, but rubber and sawn logs production will decline. Labour shortages and suitable land are constraints in the agriculture sector, the report said.

While natural gas output will show continued growth, crude oil production will decline in adherence to Malaysia's national depletion policy. Tin is also expected to continue its long-term trend of declining production.
